subjects.title: JavaScript
subjects.description: Core JavaScript language features and runtime behavior

cards.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
cards.answer: The window between entering a scope and the point where a `let`/`const` declaration is evaluated. The binding already exists but reading or writing it throws a `ReferenceError`. `var` has no TDZ — it is hoisted and initialized to `undefined`.

pt.question: O que é a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
pt.answer: A janela entre entrar em um escopo e o ponto onde uma declaração `let`/`const` é avaliada. O binding já existe, mas ler ou escrever nele lança um `ReferenceError`. `var` não tem TDZ — é içada e inicializada como `undefined`.

hints: It only applies to `let` and `const`, not `var`.

cards.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
cards.answer: `undefined` means a variable was declared but never assigned (the default absence). `null` is an intentional "no value" you assign yourself. `typeof undefined` is `"undefined"`, but `typeof null` is `"object"`. `null == undefined` is `true`; `null === undefined` is `false`.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre `null` e `undefined`?
pt.answer: `undefined` significa que uma variável foi declarada mas nunca recebeu valor (a ausência padrão). `null` é um "sem valor" intencional que você atribui. `typeof undefined` é `"undefined"`, mas `typeof null` é `"object"`. `null == undefined` é `true`; `null === undefined` é `false`.

cards.question: What is the difference between `slice` and `splice` on arrays?
cards.answer: `slice(start, end)` returns a shallow copy of a portion and **does not** mutate the array. `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` **mutates** the array in place (removing and/or inserting) and returns the removed elements.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre `slice` e `splice` em arrays?
pt.answer: `slice(start, end)` retorna uma cópia rasa de uma porção e **não** muta o array. `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` **muta** o array no lugar (removendo e/ou inserindo) e retorna os elementos removidos.

hints: One of them mutates the original.

cards.question: What does `Array.prototype.reduce` do?
cards.answer:
It folds an array into a single value by running a reducer `(acc, cur) => ...` left to right, threading an accumulator.

```javascript
[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // 10
```
With no initial value the first element seeds the accumulator (and an empty array throws).

pt.question: O que o `Array.prototype.reduce` faz?
pt.answer:
Reduz um array a um único valor executando um reducer `(acc, cur) => ...` da esquerda para a direita, propagando um acumulador.

```javascript
[1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // 10
```
Sem valor inicial, o primeiro elemento inicia o acumulador (e um array vazio lança erro).

cards.question: What is the difference between `map` and `forEach`?
cards.answer: `map` returns a **new array** of the callback's return values (a transform). `forEach` returns `undefined` and exists only for side effects. Neither mutates the source array unless your callback does.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre `map` e `forEach`?
pt.answer: `map` retorna um **novo array** com os valores retornados pelo callback (uma transformação). `forEach` retorna `undefined` e existe só para efeitos colaterais. Nenhum dos dois muta o array de origem, a menos que seu callback o faça.

cards.question: What is event delegation?
cards.answer: Attaching one listener to a common ancestor and using event **bubbling** plus `event.target` to handle events from many descendants. Benefits: fewer listeners and it automatically covers elements added later.

pt.question: O que é event delegation (delegação de eventos)?
pt.answer: Anexar um único listener a um ancestral comum e usar o **bubbling** de eventos mais `event.target` para tratar eventos de muitos descendentes. Vantagens: menos listeners e cobre automaticamente elementos adicionados depois.

cards.question: What is the event loop?
cards.answer: The mechanism that lets single-threaded JS handle async work. The call stack runs synchronous code; when it empties, the loop pulls queued callbacks. The whole **microtask** queue (Promises) drains before the next **macrotask** (timers, I/O).

pt.question: O que é o event loop?
pt.answer: O mecanismo que permite ao JS de thread única lidar com trabalho assíncrono. A call stack executa o código síncrono; quando esvazia, o loop puxa os callbacks enfileirados. Toda a fila de **microtasks** (Promises) é drenada antes da próxima **macrotask** (timers, I/O).

cards.question: What is the difference between a microtask and a macrotask?
cards.answer: **Microtasks** (Promise reactions, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) run right after the current task and the entire microtask queue drains before anything else. **Macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O, UI events) run one per event-loop turn. So a resolved Promise's `.then` runs before a `setTimeout(…, 0)`.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre uma microtask e uma macrotask?
pt.answer: **Microtasks** (reações de Promise, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) rodam logo após a tarefa atual, e toda a fila de microtasks é drenada antes de qualquer outra coisa. **Macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O, eventos de UI) rodam uma por volta do event loop. Por isso o `.then` de uma Promise resolvida roda antes de um `setTimeout(…, 0)`.

cards.question: How does `Promise.all` differ from `Promise.allSettled`?
cards.answer: `Promise.all` is **fail-fast**: it rejects as soon as any input rejects, otherwise resolves to an array of values. `Promise.allSettled` **never rejects**: it waits for every input and resolves to `{ status, value | reason }` objects, so you can inspect each outcome.

pt.question: Como o `Promise.all` difere do `Promise.allSettled`?
pt.answer: `Promise.all` é **fail-fast**: rejeita assim que qualquer entrada rejeitar; caso contrário resolve para um array de valores. `Promise.allSettled` **nunca rejeita**: espera todas as entradas e resolve para objetos `{ status, value | reason }`, então você pode inspecionar cada resultado.

cards.question: What is the prototype chain?
cards.answer: Every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link. A property lookup walks up the chain until the key is found or the chain ends at `null`. This is how inheritance works in JS. Read the link with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`; it usually ends at `Object.prototype` then `null`.

pt.question: O que é a prototype chain (cadeia de protótipos)?
pt.answer: Todo objeto tem um link interno `[[Prototype]]`. Uma busca de propriedade sobe a cadeia até achar a chave ou terminar em `null`. É assim que a herança funciona em JS. Leia o link com `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`; geralmente termina em `Object.prototype` e depois `null`.

cards.question: What does `Object.freeze` do?
cards.answer: Makes an object immutable: you can't add, remove, or reassign its properties (silently ignored in sloppy mode, throws in strict mode). It is **shallow** — nested objects stay mutable unless you freeze them too.

pt.question: O que o `Object.freeze` faz?
pt.answer: Torna um objeto imutável: você não pode adicionar, remover ou reatribuir suas propriedades (ignorado silenciosamente no modo sloppy, lança erro no strict mode). É **raso** — objetos aninhados continuam mutáveis a menos que você os congele também.

cards.question: What is destructuring assignment?

pt.question: O que é destructuring assignment (atribuição por desestruturação)?

cards.question: What is the difference between `for...in` and `for...of`?
cards.answer: `for...in` iterates enumerable **keys**, including inherited ones — meant for objects, but use with care. `for...of` iterates **values** of any iterable (arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set`). For arrays, prefer `for...of`.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre `for...in` e `for...of`?
pt.answer: `for...in` itera **chaves** enumeráveis, incluindo as herdadas — feito para objetos, mas use com cuidado. `for...of` itera **valores** de qualquer iterável (arrays, strings, `Map`, `Set`). Para arrays, prefira `for...of`.

cards.question: What is the difference between spread and rest?
cards.answer: Same `...` token, opposite jobs. **Spread** expands an iterable or object into individual elements/props (in calls and literals). **Rest** collects the remaining items into an array/object (in parameters and destructuring).

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre spread e rest?
pt.answer: Mesmo token `...`, papéis opostos. **Spread** expande um iterável ou objeto em elementos/propriedades individuais (em chamadas e literais). **Rest** coleta os itens restantes em um array/objeto (em parâmetros e desestruturação).

cards.question: What is currying?
cards.answer: Transforming a function of N arguments into N nested unary functions, each returning the next: `f(a)(b)(c)`. It enables partial application and easy composition.

pt.question: O que é currying?
pt.answer: Transformar uma função de N argumentos em N funções unárias aninhadas, cada uma retornando a próxima: `f(a)(b)(c)`. Permite aplicação parcial e composição fácil.

cards.question: What is memoization?
cards.answer: Caching a function's results keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return the cached value instead of recomputing. It trades memory for speed and only works for **pure** functions.

pt.question: O que é memoization?
pt.answer: Cachear os resultados de uma função indexados pelos seus argumentos, para que chamadas repetidas com as mesmas entradas retornem o valor em cache em vez de recalcular. Troca memória por velocidade e só funciona para funções **puras**.

cards.question: What is the difference between `call`, `apply`, and `bind`?
cards.answer: All three set `this`. `call(thisArg, ...args)` invokes immediately with args listed individually. `apply(thisArg, argsArray)` invokes immediately with args as an array. `bind(thisArg, ...args)` returns a **new** function with `this` (and any preset args) permanently bound, without calling it.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre `call`, `apply` e `bind`?
pt.answer: Os três definem `this`. `call(thisArg, ...args)` invoca imediatamente com os argumentos listados individualmente. `apply(thisArg, argsArray)` invoca imediatamente com os argumentos como array. `bind(thisArg, ...args)` retorna uma **nova** função com `this` (e quaisquer argumentos pré-definidos) permanentemente vinculados, sem chamá-la.

cards.question: What is a Promise and what states can it be in?
cards.answer: An object representing a value that may be available later. States: **pending** → either **fulfilled** (with a value) or **rejected** (with a reason). Settling is one-way and final. You react with `.then` / `.catch` / `.finally`.

pt.question: O que é uma Promise e em quais estados ela pode estar?
pt.answer: Um objeto que representa um valor que pode estar disponível depois. Estados: **pending** → ou **fulfilled** (com um valor) ou **rejected** (com um motivo). A resolução é unidirecional e final. Você reage com `.then` / `.catch` / `.finally`.

cards.question: What do `async` and `await` do?
cards.answer: `async` makes a function always return a Promise. `await` pauses the function until a Promise settles, yielding its value (or throwing its rejection), letting you write async code in a synchronous style. Handle errors with `try/catch`.

pt.question: O que `async` e `await` fazem?
pt.answer: `async` faz uma função sempre retornar uma Promise. `await` pausa a função até uma Promise se resolver, devolvendo seu valor (ou lançando sua rejeição), permitindo escrever código assíncrono em estilo síncrono. Trate erros com `try/catch`.

cards.question: What is optional chaining (`?.`)?
cards.answer: It short-circuits and returns `undefined` when a reference is `null` or `undefined`, instead of throwing. Works for property access, indexing, and calls: `a?.b`, `a?.[i]`, `fn?.()`.

pt.question: O que é optional chaining (`?.`)?
pt.answer: Faz curto-circuito e retorna `undefined` quando uma referência é `null` ou `undefined`, em vez de lançar erro. Funciona para acesso a propriedade, indexação e chamadas: `a?.b`, `a?.[i]`, `fn?.()`.

cards.question: What is the nullish coalescing operator (`??`)?
cards.answer:
It returns the right operand only when the left is `null` or `undefined` — not for other falsy values like `0` or `''`. Contrast with `||`, which falls back on **any** falsy value.

```javascript
0 ?? 5;  // 0
0 || 5;  // 5
```

pt.question: O que é o operador de nullish coalescing (`??`)?
pt.answer:
Retorna o operando da direita apenas quando o da esquerda é `null` ou `undefined` — não para outros valores falsy como `0` ou `''`. Compare com `||`, que recorre ao fallback para **qualquer** valor falsy.

```javascript
0 ?? 5;  // 0
0 || 5;  // 5
```

cards.question: What are template literals?
cards.answer: Backtick strings that support multi-line text and `${expression}` interpolation. They also enable **tagged templates**, where a function receives the string parts and the interpolated values separately.

pt.question: O que são template literals?
pt.answer: Strings com crase que suportam texto multilinha e interpolação `${expression}`. Também habilitam **tagged templates**, onde uma função recebe as partes da string e os valores interpolados separadamente.

cards.question: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?
cards.answer: A **shallow** copy duplicates only the top level and shares nested references (`{...obj}`, `Object.assign`, `arr.slice()`). A **deep** copy recursively clones everything (`structuredClone`, or `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` with caveats).

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre uma cópia rasa (shallow) e uma profunda (deep)?
pt.answer: Uma cópia **rasa** duplica só o nível superior e compartilha referências aninhadas (`{...obj}`, `Object.assign`, `arr.slice()`). Uma cópia **profunda** clona tudo recursivamente (`structuredClone`, ou `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` com ressalvas).

cards.question: What is `structuredClone`?
cards.answer: A built-in that **deep-clones** most values — objects, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, typed arrays, and even cyclic references. It cannot clone functions, DOM nodes, or prototype chains (those throw or are dropped).

pt.question: O que é `structuredClone`?
pt.answer: Uma função nativa que faz **clone profundo** da maioria dos valores — objetos, arrays, `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, typed arrays e até referências cíclicas. Não consegue clonar funções, nós do DOM ou cadeias de protótipo (esses lançam erro ou são descartados).

cards.question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
cards.answer: A **declaration** (`function f() {}`) is fully hoisted, so it's callable before its line. An **expression** (`const f = function () {}`) is not — only the variable binding hoists per `var`/`let` rules. Arrow functions are always expressions.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre uma function declaration e uma function expression?
pt.answer: Uma **declaration** (`function f() {}`) é totalmente hoisted, então pode ser chamada antes da sua linha. Uma **expression** (`const f = function () {}`) não — só a vinculação da variável é hoisted, conforme as regras de `var`/`let`. Arrow functions são sempre expressions.

cards.question: What are the falsy values in JavaScript?
cards.answer: Exactly eight: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy — including `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]`, and `{}`.

pt.question: Quais são os valores falsy em JavaScript?
pt.answer: Exatamente oito: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''` (string vazia), `null`, `undefined` e `NaN`. Todo o resto é truthy — incluindo `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]` e `{}`.

hints: There are eight of them.

cards.question: How do a `Map` and a plain object differ?

pt.question: Como um `Map` difere de um objeto comum?

cards.question: What is a `Set`?
cards.answer: A collection of **unique** values (compared with SameValueZero). It has fast `add`/`has`/`delete`, a `size`, and iterates in insertion order. Common trick: dedupe an array with `[...new Set(arr)]`.

pt.question: O que é um `Set`?
pt.answer: Uma coleção de valores **únicos** (comparados com SameValueZero). Tem `add`/`has`/`delete` rápidos, um `size`, e itera na ordem de inserção. Truque comum: remover duplicatas de um array com `[...new Set(arr)]`.

cards.question: What do `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, and `Object.entries` return?
cards.answer: All three return arrays over an object's **own enumerable string-keyed** properties: `keys` → the keys, `values` → the values, `entries` → `[key, value]` pairs (handy with `for...of` and `Object.fromEntries`).

pt.question: O que `Object.keys`, `Object.values` e `Object.entries` retornam?
pt.answer: Os três retornam arrays sobre as propriedades **próprias, enumeráveis e com chave string** de um objeto: `keys` → as chaves, `values` → os valores, `entries` → pares `[chave, valor]` (úteis com `for...of` e `Object.fromEntries`).

cards.question: What is short-circuit evaluation?
cards.answer: `&&` returns the first **falsy** operand (or the last operand if all are truthy); `||` returns the first **truthy** operand (or the last if all are falsy). Evaluation stops once the result is determined — used for guards and defaults.

pt.question: O que é short-circuit evaluation (avaliação por curto-circuito)?
pt.answer: `&&` retorna o primeiro operando **falsy** (ou o último, se todos forem truthy); `||` retorna o primeiro operando **truthy** (ou o último, se todos forem falsy). A avaliação para assim que o resultado é determinado — usado para guardas e defaults.

cards.question: What is the difference between `throw`ing an error and returning one?
cards.answer: `throw` unwinds the call stack until a `try/catch` handles it (or the program crashes), interrupting control flow. Returning an error value keeps normal control flow and forces the caller to check the result. Both are valid; pick per API style.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre lançar (`throw`) um erro e retorná-lo?
pt.answer: `throw` desenrola a call stack até que um `try/catch` o trate (ou o programa quebra), interrompendo o fluxo de controle. Retornar um valor de erro mantém o fluxo normal e força o chamador a verificar o resultado. Ambos são válidos; escolha conforme o estilo da API.

cards.question: What does the `new` operator do?
cards.answer: Four steps: (1) create a fresh object, (2) link its `[[Prototype]]` to the constructor's `.prototype`, (3) bind `this` to it and run the constructor body, (4) return that object — unless the constructor explicitly returns its own object.

pt.question: O que o operador `new` faz?
pt.answer: Quatro passos: (1) cria um objeto novo, (2) liga seu `[[Prototype]]` ao `.prototype` do construtor, (3) vincula `this` a ele e roda o corpo do construtor, (4) retorna esse objeto — a menos que o construtor retorne explicitamente seu próprio objeto.

cards.question: What is a `Symbol` used for?
cards.answer: A primitive that produces **unique**, collision-free identifiers. Common uses: non-enumerable object keys and well-known protocols like `Symbol.iterator` (which makes a value iterable) and `Symbol.asyncIterator`.

pt.question: Para que serve um `Symbol`?
pt.answer: Um primitivo que produz identificadores **únicos** e livres de colisão. Usos comuns: chaves de objeto não enumeráveis e protocolos bem conhecidos como `Symbol.iterator` (que torna um valor iterável) e `Symbol.asyncIterator`.

cards.question: What is the difference between `Object.create(null)` and `{}`?
cards.answer: `{}` inherits from `Object.prototype`, so it has `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, etc. `Object.create(null)` has **no prototype** — a bare dictionary with no inherited keys, immune to prototype-pollution and key collisions like a `"toString"` key.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre `Object.create(null)` e `{}`?
pt.answer: `{}` herda de `Object.prototype`, então tem `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` etc. `Object.create(null)` **não tem prototype** — um dicionário puro, sem chaves herdadas, imune a prototype-pollution e a colisões de chave como uma chave `"toString"`.

cards.question: What does `typeof NaN` return?
cards.answer: `NaN` ("Not a Number") is itself a value of the number type, so `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.

pt.question: O que `typeof NaN` retorna?
pt.answer: `NaN` ("Not a Number") é, ele mesmo, um valor do tipo number, então `typeof NaN` é `"number"`.

cards.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2)` return?
cards.answer: `map` returns a new array of each callback result.

pt.question: O que `[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2)` retorna?
pt.answer: `map` retorna um novo array com cada resultado do callback.

cards.question: What does `'5' + 3` evaluate to?
cards.answer: With a string operand, `+` concatenates: the number `3` is coerced to `"3"`, giving `"53"`.

pt.question: Quanto vale `'5' + 3`?
pt.answer: Com um operando string, `+` concatena: o número `3` é convertido para `"3"`, resultando em `"53"`.

cards.question: What does `'5' - 3` evaluate to?
cards.answer: `-` has no string meaning, so `'5'` is coerced to the number `5`, giving `2`.

pt.question: Quanto vale `'5' - 3`?
pt.answer: `-` não tem significado para strings, então `'5'` é convertido para o número `5`, resultando em `2`.

cards.question: What does `typeof function () {}` return?
cards.answer: Functions are callable objects, but `typeof` reports them specially as `"function"`.

pt.question: O que `typeof function () {}` retorna?
pt.answer: Funções são objetos chamáveis, mas `typeof` as reporta de forma especial como `"function"`.

cards.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].indexOf(4)` return?
cards.answer: `indexOf` returns `-1` when the value is not found.

pt.question: O que `[1, 2, 3].indexOf(4)` retorna?
pt.answer: `indexOf` retorna `-1` quando o valor não é encontrado.

cards.question: What does `Boolean('')` return?
cards.answer: An empty string is one of the eight falsy values.

pt.question: O que `Boolean('')` retorna?
pt.answer: Uma string vazia é um dos oito valores falsy.

cards.question: What does `Boolean('0')` return?
cards.answer: Any non-empty string is truthy — including `'0'`, `'false'`, and `' '`.

pt.question: O que `Boolean('0')` retorna?
pt.answer: Qualquer string não vazia é truthy — incluindo `'0'`, `'false'` e `' '`.

cards.question: What does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` return?
cards.answer: The default `sort` converts elements to strings and compares lexicographically: `"1" < "10" < "9"`. Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)` for numbers.

pt.question: O que `[10, 9, 1].sort()` retorna?
pt.answer: O `sort` padrão converte os elementos em strings e compara lexicograficamente: `"1" < "10" < "9"`. Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)` para números.

cards.question: What does `Promise.resolve(1).then(x => x + 1)` resolve to?
cards.answer: `.then` returns a new Promise resolved with the callback's return value, `2`.

pt.question: Para que valor `Promise.resolve(1).then(x => x + 1)` resolve?
pt.answer: `.then` retorna uma nova Promise resolvida com o valor retornado pelo callback, `2`.

cards.answer: Synchronous code runs first (`A`, `D`). Then the microtask (`C`) drains before the `setTimeout` macrotask (`B`).

pt.answer: O código síncrono roda primeiro (`A`, `D`). Depois a microtask (`C`) é drenada antes da macrotask do `setTimeout` (`B`).

cards.question: What does `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0)` return?
cards.answer: `filter` keeps the elements for which the callback is truthy — the even numbers.

pt.question: O que `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0)` retorna?
pt.answer: `filter` mantém os elementos para os quais o callback é truthy — os números pares.

cards.question: What does `0 == ''` evaluate to?
cards.answer: Loose equality coerces both sides to numbers: `''` becomes `0`, so `0 == 0` is `true`. `0 === ''` would be `false`.

pt.question: Quanto vale `0 == ''`?
pt.answer: A igualdade frouxa converte ambos os lados para números: `''` vira `0`, então `0 == 0` é `true`. `0 === ''` seria `false`.

cards.question: What does `NaN === NaN` evaluate to?
cards.answer: `NaN` is never equal to anything, including itself. Detect it with `Number.isNaN`.

pt.question: Quanto vale `NaN === NaN`?
pt.answer: `NaN` nunca é igual a nada, incluindo a si mesmo. Detecte-o com `Number.isNaN`.

cards.question: What does `parseInt('08px', 10)` return?
cards.answer: `parseInt` reads leading characters that form a valid integer and stops at the first invalid one, giving `8`.

pt.question: O que `parseInt('08px', 10)` retorna?
pt.answer: `parseInt` lê os caracteres iniciais que formam um inteiro válido e para no primeiro inválido, resultando em `8`.

cards.question: What does `[...'abc']` produce?
cards.answer: Strings are iterable, so spreading yields an array of characters.

pt.question: O que `[...'abc']` produz?
pt.answer: Strings são iteráveis, então o spread gera um array de caracteres.

cards.question: What does `JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` return?
cards.answer: `JSON.stringify` omits properties whose value is `undefined` (and functions).

pt.question: O que `JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` retorna?
pt.answer: `JSON.stringify` omite propriedades cujo valor é `undefined` (e funções).

cards.question: What does `typeof []` return?
cards.answer: Arrays are objects, so `typeof []` is `"object"`. Use `Array.isArray` to detect arrays.

pt.question: O que `typeof []` retorna?
pt.answer: Arrays são objetos, então `typeof []` é `"object"`. Use `Array.isArray` para detectar arrays.

cards.question: What does `1 < 2 < 3` evaluate to?
cards.answer: It evaluates left to right: `(1 < 2)` is `true`, then `true < 3` coerces `true` to `1`, and `1 < 3` is `true`. (Beware: `3 < 2 < 1` is also `true`.)

pt.question: Quanto vale `1 < 2 < 3`?
pt.answer: Avalia da esquerda para a direita: `(1 < 2)` é `true`, então `true < 3` converte `true` para `1`, e `1 < 3` é `true`. (Cuidado: `3 < 2 < 1` também é `true`.)

cards.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) and which declarations does it affect?
cards.answer:
The TDZ is the period between entering a block scope and the point where a `let` or `const` declaration is evaluated. Accessing the binding during this period throws a `ReferenceError`. It affects `let` and `const` (but not `var`). Example:
```js
console.log(x); // ReferenceError
let x = 5;
```
hints: Think about what happens before the declaration line is reached.

cards.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
cards.answer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its outer (enclosing) lexical scope even after that outer function has finished executing. The inner function "closes over" those variables, keeping them alive as long as the closure exists.

cards.question: What is the **default binding** rule for `this` in a plain function call (non-strict mode)?
cards.answer: In non-strict mode, when a function is called without any explicit receiver, `this` defaults to the global object (`window` in browsers, `global` in Node.js). In strict mode (`'use strict'`), `this` is `undefined` instead.

cards.question: What is the prototype chain in JavaScript, and how does property lookup work along it?
cards.answer: Every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link that points to another object (or `null`). When you access a property, the engine first checks the object itself, then walks up the chain through each `[[Prototype]]` until the property is found or `null` is reached. Example: `obj.toString()` is typically found on `Object.prototype` at the end of the chain.
hints: Think of it as a linked list of objects

cards.question: What is the difference between a class declaration and a class expression in JavaScript?
cards.answer: Both define a class. A class declaration (`class Foo {}`) creates a hoisted binding that is in the temporal dead zone until evaluation, so it can't be used before its declaration. A class expression (`const Foo = class {}`) can be anonymous or named, and is convenient for assigning classes dynamically or passing them as values.
hints: Think about how `function` declarations vs expressions differ, but note classes are NOT hoisted the same way — they sit in a temporal dead zone.

cards.question: What are the seven primitive types in JavaScript (ES2020+)?
cards.answer: The seven primitives are: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, and `symbol`. They are not objects and have no methods of their own.
hints: One was added in ES2015, another in ES2020

cards.question: What is the difference between `==` (abstract equality) and `===` (strict equality) in JavaScript?
cards.answer: `===` compares both value and type with no coercion — if the types differ, it returns `false` immediately. `==` performs type coercion first (following the Abstract Equality Comparison algorithm) before comparing values, so `1 == '1'` is `true` but `1 === '1'` is `false`.
hints: One converts types; the other does not.

cards.question: Why does `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` evaluate to `false` in JavaScript?
cards.answer: JavaScript uses IEEE-754 double-precision floating point, which cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly in binary. Their sum is approximately `0.30000000000000004`, not exactly `0.3`. To compare floats, use an epsilon check: `Math.abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON`.
hints: Think about how decimals are stored in binary.

cards.question: Why are JavaScript strings said to be *immutable*? What does that mean in practice?
cards.answer: Once a string is created, its characters cannot be changed in place. Any operation that appears to "modify" a string (like `replace`, `toUpperCase`, or concatenation) always returns a *new* string; the original is untouched. For example, `let s = 'hello'; s[0] = 'H';` has no effect — `s` is still `'hello'`.
hints: What happens when you assign to a character index?

cards.question: What is the difference between mutating and non-mutating array methods? Give one example of each.
cards.answer: Mutating methods modify the original array in place (e.g., `push`, `splice`, `sort`). Non-mutating methods return a new array or value without changing the original (e.g., `map`, `filter`, `slice`). For example, `arr.push(4)` changes `arr`, while `arr.concat([4])` returns a new array leaving `arr` unchanged.
hints: Think about whether the original array changes after the call.

cards.question: What are the four attributes that make up a data property descriptor in JavaScript?
cards.answer: A data property descriptor has four attributes: `value` (the property's value), `writable` (whether the value can be changed), `enumerable` (whether it appears in `for...in` loops and `Object.keys()`), and `configurable` (whether the property can be deleted or its descriptor changed).
hints: Think about what you can control when using Object.defineProperty

cards.question: What are default parameters in JavaScript, and when is the default value evaluated?
hints: Think about what value triggers the default

cards.question: What are the three possible states of a Promise, and can a Promise transition between them freely?
cards.answer: A Promise can be **pending** (initial state, neither fulfilled nor rejected), **fulfilled** (operation completed successfully), or **rejected** (operation failed). Transitions are one-way only: a pending promise can become fulfilled or rejected, but once settled it is immutable and cannot change state again.
hints: Think of a one-way door

cards.question: What is the iterator protocol in JavaScript, and what two properties must an iterator object expose?
cards.answer: The iterator protocol defines a standard way to produce a sequence of values. An iterator object must expose a `next()` method that returns an object with two properties: `value` (the yielded value) and `done` (a boolean — `true` when the sequence is exhausted, `false` otherwise).
hints: Think about what `next()` returns.

cards.question: What key equality algorithm does `Map` use when comparing keys, and how does it differ from `===`?
cards.answer: Map uses the **SameValueZero** algorithm. It behaves like `===` except that `NaN` is treated as equal to itself under SameValueZero, so `NaN` can be used as a Map key and two `NaN` keys are treated as identical. Everything else matches `===`, including `-0` and `+0` being equal and objects compared by reference.
hints: Think about how NaN compares to itself

cards.question: What makes every `Symbol()` call produce a unique value, and what does that mean in practice?
cards.answer: Each call to `Symbol()` allocates a brand-new symbol that is guaranteed to be unequal to every other symbol ever created — even if given the same description. So `Symbol('x') === Symbol('x')` is `false`. This uniqueness is the core reason symbols are used as non-colliding property keys.

cards.question: What is a **live binding** in ES modules, and how does it differ from CommonJS exports?
cards.answer: An ES module live binding means an imported name reflects the *current* value of the exporting module's variable — if the exporter reassigns it, all importers see the new value. CommonJS `require()` copies the value at the time of the call, so reassigning a primitive on `module.exports.x` later does **not** update what the consumer already captured into a local variable.
hints: Think about what happens when the exporting module calls `setTimeout` and changes a variable after the import runs.

cards.question: What is the difference between `throw new Error('msg')` and `throw 'msg'` in JavaScript?
cards.answer: Both are syntactically valid — JavaScript lets you throw any value. However, throwing a non-`Error` value means you lose the stack trace and the standard `.message`/`.name` properties. Catching code that expects `err.message` will get `undefined` if a plain string was thrown. Best practice is always to `throw new Error(...)` or a subclass.
hints: Only Error instances have a `.stack` property

cards.question: What happens to `undefined`, functions, and `Symbol` values when you pass them to `JSON.stringify`?
cards.answer: They are **dropped** (omitted) from the output. As an object property value, the whole key-value pair is removed. As an array element, it becomes `null` to preserve indices. A top-level `undefined`, function, or symbol makes `JSON.stringify` return the value `undefined` (not a string).
hints: Think separately about object properties vs. array slots.

cards.question: How does `var` hoisting differ from `let`/`const` hoisting?
cards.answer: `var` declarations are hoisted to the top of their function (or global) scope and initialized to `undefined`, so reading them before the declaration yields `undefined`. `let` and `const` are also hoisted to the top of their block, but they are **not** initialized — accessing them before the declaration throws a `ReferenceError` due to the TDZ.
hints: Both are hoisted, but initialization differs.

cards.question: Why do closures capture variables **by reference** rather than by value?
What is **implicit binding** and when is it lost?
cards.answer: Implicit binding occurs when a function is called as a method on an object — `obj.fn()` — making `this` refer to `obj`. It is lost when the method reference is detached from the object, such as `const fn = obj.method; fn();`, which reverts to default binding (`this` becomes the global object, or `undefined` in strict mode).
hints: Think about what happens when you pass a method as a callback.

cards.question: What is the difference between `__proto__` and `prototype` in JavaScript?
cards.answer: `__proto__` is a legacy accessor (defined on `Object.prototype`) that reads/writes an object's `[[Prototype]]` link, pointing to its prototype object. `prototype` is a property that exists only on functions, and it becomes the `[[Prototype]]` of objects created with `new ThatFunction()`. So `obj.__proto__ === Constructor.prototype` for instances created via `new`. (Prefer `Object.getPrototypeOf`/`Object.setPrototypeOf` over `__proto__`.)
hints: `__proto__` is on instances; `prototype` is on constructor functions

cards.question: What are public instance fields and how do they differ from properties set inside the `constructor`?
cards.answer: Public instance fields are declared in the class body (e.g., `count = 0;`) and are added to each instance using define semantics (like `Object.defineProperty`) before the constructor body runs. Properties set inside the constructor (`this.count = 0`) are assigned imperatively during construction. Both become own properties, but fields are declarative and can be listed without writing a constructor.

cards.question: What is autoboxing in JavaScript, and when does it happen?
cards.answer: Autoboxing is the automatic (temporary) wrapping of a primitive value in its corresponding wrapper object when you access a property or method on it. For example, `'hello'.toUpperCase()` temporarily wraps `'hello'` in a `String` object to call the method, then discards the wrapper. The original primitive remains unchanged.
hints: The wrapper is discarded immediately after the property access

cards.question: What is the `ToPrimitive` abstract operation and when does JavaScript invoke it?
cards.answer: `ToPrimitive(input, preferredType)` converts an object to a primitive. JavaScript calls it when an object appears where a primitive is expected (e.g., arithmetic, string concatenation, loose equality). It tries `[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint)` first; if absent, falls back to `valueOf()` then `toString()` for the `'number'` hint, or `toString()` then `valueOf()` for the `'string'` hint.
hints: It checks Symbol.toPrimitive first.

cards.question: What is `Number.EPSILON` and what is it used for?
cards.answer: `Number.EPSILON` is the difference between `1` and the smallest double greater than `1`, approximately `2.220446049250313e-16`. It is commonly used as a relative tolerance threshold when comparing floating-point numbers for near-equality, e.g. `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` (note: a fixed epsilon only works well for values near 1; large magnitudes need a scaled tolerance).

cards.question: What is the difference between `String.prototype.slice` and `String.prototype.substring` when negative indices are passed?
cards.answer: `slice` treats negative indices as offsets from the end of the string (`'hello'.slice(-3)` → `'llo'`). `substring` treats any negative argument as `0`, so `'hello'.substring(-3)` is equivalent to `'hello'.substring(0)` → `'hello'`. Both accept `(start, end)` parameters and return up to but not including `end`.

cards.question: How does `Array.prototype.reduce` work, and what is the role of the initial value argument?
cards.answer: `reduce(callback, initialValue)` iterates over the array, passing an accumulator and current element to the callback each time, and returns the final accumulated result. If `initialValue` is provided, the accumulator starts as that value and iteration begins at index 0. Without it, the accumulator is the first element and iteration starts at index 1 — on an empty array with no initial value, a `TypeError` is thrown.

cards.question: What is the difference between `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()`?
cards.answer: `Object.seal()` prevents adding or deleting properties but still allows modifying existing writable properties. `Object.freeze()` does everything `seal()` does AND also sets all data properties to non-writable, making the object effectively immutable at the top level. Neither is deep/recursive.
hints: One prevents adds/deletes, the other also prevents writes

cards.question: What is a rest parameter, and how does it differ from the `arguments` object?
hints: Consider arrow functions

cards.question: What is the difference between returning a value and throwing inside a `.then()` callback?
cards.answer:
Returning a value inside `.then()` settles the resulting promise as fulfilled with that value, passing it to the next `.then()` in the chain. Throwing an error (or returning a rejected promise) causes the resulting promise to reject, so the chain skips subsequent `.then()` fulfillment handlers and jumps to the nearest `.catch()`. Example:
```js
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then(v => { throw new Error('oops'); })
  .catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // 'oops'
```

cards.question: What does `await` actually do to execution inside an `async` function?
cards.answer: `await expr` suspends the async function, schedules a microtask to resume it when `expr` settles, and immediately returns control to the caller. If `expr` is already a fulfilled Promise, resumption is still deferred as a microtask — it never resumes synchronously.
hints: Think of await as a yield point that always defers to the microtask queue.

cards.question: What is the difference between an *iterable* and an *iterator* in JavaScript?
cards.answer: An **iterable** is any object with a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method that returns an iterator. An **iterator** is an object with a `next()` method that follows the iterator protocol. A single object can be both (e.g., generators) by returning `this` from `[Symbol.iterator]()`.
hints: One has `Symbol.iterator`, the other has `next()`.

cards.question: Does `Map` guarantee iteration order? If so, what order?
cards.answer: Yes. A `Map` iterates entries in **insertion order** — the order in which keys were first added. This guarantee is part of the ES2015 spec and applies to `map.keys()`, `map.values()`, `map.entries()`, and `map.forEach()`.

cards.question: What is the global symbol registry, and how do `Symbol.for()` and `Symbol.keyFor()` interact with it?
cards.answer: `Symbol.for(key)` looks up a string key in a single, cross-realm registry. If a symbol with that key already exists it is returned; otherwise a new one is created and stored. `Symbol.keyFor(sym)` performs the reverse: given a symbol, it returns the string key under which it was registered, or `undefined` if the symbol was not created via `Symbol.for()`.

cards.question: What is the difference between a **named export** and a **default export** in ES modules?
cards.answer: A named export is bound to a specific identifier: `export const foo = 1`. It must be imported using the same name (or aliased). A default export — `export default value` — is the module's primary export; it is imported without curly braces and can be given any local name: `import anything from './mod.js'`. A module may have many named exports but only **one** default export.

cards.question: What does the `finally` block guarantee, and what happens if it contains a `return` statement?
cards.answer: The `finally` block always runs after `try` (and `catch`, if triggered), regardless of whether an error was thrown or a `return`/`break`/`continue` was used. If `finally` itself contains a `return`, that value **overrides** any `return` value or thrown error from the `try` or `catch` block — the original outcome is silently discarded.
hints: A return inside finally swallows thrown errors

cards.question: What is the `replacer` argument of `JSON.stringify`, and what are its two forms?
cards.answer: The `replacer` controls which values are serialised. It can be (1) a **function** `(key, value) => …` — return `undefined` to omit a key, or a transformed value to include it — or (2) an **array of strings/numbers** that acts as an allowlist of property names to include.

cards.question: What is the difference between block scope and function scope in JavaScript?
cards.answer: Function scope means a variable declared with `var` is accessible anywhere within the enclosing function (and nested functions). Block scope means a variable declared with `let` or `const` is only accessible within the nearest enclosing `{}` block. A `var` inside an `if` block leaks out; a `let` does not.

cards.question: What is the classic closure-in-loop bug, and why does it occur?
How does `new` binding determine the value of `this`?
cards.answer: When a function is called with `new`, a brand-new empty object is created, `this` inside the constructor is bound to that new object, and the object is returned automatically (unless the function explicitly returns a different object). This is called **new binding** and takes priority over explicit binding.

cards.question: How does `Object.create(proto)` differ from using `new Constructor()` to set up a prototype?
cards.answer: `Object.create(proto)` creates a new object whose `[[Prototype]]` is set directly to `proto`, without calling any constructor function. `new Constructor()` creates an object whose `[[Prototype]]` is `Constructor.prototype` and also runs the constructor body. `Object.create(null)` produces an object with no prototype at all.
hints: One runs a constructor; the other does not

cards.question: How do `#private` fields differ from convention-based `_private` properties?
cards.answer: `#private` fields are enforced by the JavaScript engine — they are lexically scoped to the class body and cannot be accessed or even detected from outside the class. `_private` is merely a naming convention with no enforcement; any code can still read or write `obj._value`.

cards.question: Why can't you add a property to a primitive string in JavaScript?
cards.answer: Primitives are immutable and not true objects. When you write `let s = 'hi'; s.foo = 1;`, autoboxing creates a temporary `String` wrapper, sets `.foo` on it, and then immediately discards the wrapper. Reading `s.foo` afterward produces `undefined` because the wrapper is gone. (In strict mode the assignment throws a TypeError.)
hints: The temporary wrapper is thrown away after each property access

cards.question: Why does `NaN === NaN` evaluate to `false`, and how can you reliably check for `NaN`?
cards.answer: By spec, `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself — both `==` and `===` return `false` for `NaN === NaN`. Use `Number.isNaN(value)` (preferred, no coercion) or `Object.is(value, NaN)` to detect `NaN` reliably. The legacy global `isNaN()` coerces its argument first, which is a common source of bugs.
hints: NaN is the only value that is not equal to itself.

cards.question: How does `BigInt` differ from the `Number` type in JavaScript, and what operator or conversion caveat should you be aware of?
cards.answer: `BigInt` (suffix `n`, e.g. `9007199254740993n`) can represent integers of arbitrary size without precision loss, while `Number` can only represent integers exactly up to `2^53 - 1` (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`). You cannot mix `BigInt` and `Number` in arithmetic expressions directly — doing so throws a `TypeError`, so you must explicitly convert one to the other. `typeof 1n === 'bigint'`.

cards.question: What are tagged template literals, and what arguments does the tag function receive?
cards.answer: A tagged template is a function call where the function (the *tag*) is placed immediately before a template literal: ``tag`text ${expr}` ``. The tag function receives: (1) an array of the literal (cooked) string segments (`strings`), then (2) each interpolated expression as subsequent arguments. `strings.raw` gives the raw, unescaped segments. This allows custom string processing, e.g., sanitizing HTML or building SQL queries.

cards.question: What does `Array.prototype.flat` do, and how does specifying a depth affect the result?
cards.answer: `flat(depth)` recursively flattens nested arrays up to the given depth (default `1`). For example, `[1, [2, [3]]].flat()` returns `[1, 2, [3]]`, while `[1, [2, [3]]].flat(Infinity)` returns `[1, 2, 3]`. It also removes holes (empty slots) in sparse arrays.
hints: Try `flat(Infinity)` for fully deep flattening.

cards.question: What does the spread operator do when used on an object, and what kind of properties does it copy?
cards.answer: The spread operator (`{ ...obj }`) creates a shallow copy of an object, copying all own enumerable properties (both string-keyed and symbol-keyed). Non-enumerable properties and inherited (prototype-chain) properties are not included, and descriptors are not preserved.

cards.question: Why can't arrow functions be used as constructors?
cards.answer: Arrow functions do not have their own `this` binding, `prototype`, or `[[Construct]]` internal slot. Calling `new` on them throws a `TypeError`. They capture `this` lexically from their enclosing scope, which makes them unsuitable for producing new objects.
hints: Think about what `new` requires

cards.answer: Output: `A`, `D`, `B`, `C`. `A` and `D` are synchronous. After the synchronous task, the microtask queue drains and logs `B`. Only then does the event loop pick the macrotask (setTimeout callback), logging `C`.

cards.question: How does `for...of` use the `Symbol.iterator` protocol internally?
cards.answer: `for...of` calls `obj[Symbol.iterator]()` once to obtain an iterator, then repeatedly calls `iterator.next()`. It assigns `result.value` to the loop variable each iteration and stops when `result.done` is `true`. This is why any object with `[Symbol.iterator]` works with `for...of`.

cards.question: What are two concrete advantages of using `Map` over a plain object `{}` as a key-value store?
cards.answer: 1. **Any value as a key**: Maps accept objects, functions, `NaN`, `null`, and primitives — plain objects only allow string and symbol keys (other keys are coerced to strings). 2. **No prototype pollution**: a plain object inherits keys like `toString` and `constructor`; a Map has no inherited entries, so iteration is always clean. (Bonus: Map has a direct `.size` and is reliably ordered.)
hints: Consider what types of keys each supports

cards.question: What is `Symbol.iterator` and how does an object use it to become iterable?
cards.answer: An object is iterable when it has a method keyed by `Symbol.iterator` that returns an iterator (an object with a `next()` method returning `{value, done}`). The `for...of` loop, spread operator, and destructuring all call this method automatically. Example: `class Range { [Symbol.iterator]() { ... } }`.

cards.question: How does `import()` (dynamic import) differ from a static `import` declaration?
cards.answer: `import()` is a function-like expression evaluated at runtime; it returns a **Promise** that resolves to the module's namespace object. Static `import` declarations are resolved at parse/link time, cannot appear inside blocks or conditions, and are hoisted to the top of the module. Dynamic import is useful for code-splitting and conditional loading: `const mod = await import('./heavy.js')`.

cards.question: How do you create a custom error class in modern JavaScript (ES2015+)?
How does the `reviver` function in `JSON.parse` work, and in what order is it called?
cards.answer: The reviver is called bottom-up (innermost values first) for every key-value pair. For each pair, returning `undefined` deletes that key from the result; any other return value replaces the original. The final call is for the root value with key `""`.

cards.question: What does it mean for a `const` binding to be 'constant', and what does it not prevent?
cards.answer: `const` prevents reassignment of the binding itself — you cannot do `x = newValue` after declaration. It does **not** make the value immutable: if the value is an object or array, its properties/elements can still be mutated. Example: `const arr = [1]; arr.push(2);` is valid.

cards.question: How do factory functions use closures to create private state?
Why does an arrow function not have its own `this`?
cards.answer: Arrow functions capture the `this` value of their **enclosing lexical scope** at the time they are defined — they have no `this` binding of their own. Because of this, `call`, `apply`, and `bind` cannot change the `this` of an arrow function.

cards.question: What does `hasOwnProperty` check, and why does it matter when iterating an object?
cards.answer: `hasOwnProperty(key)` returns `true` only if the property exists directly on the object, not inherited through the prototype chain. When using `for...in`, which iterates all enumerable properties including inherited ones, `hasOwnProperty` guards against processing prototype properties unintentionally. Modern code often uses `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` (ES2022) as a safer alternative.
hints: for...in traverses the whole chain

cards.question: What is a `static` block in a class, and what problem does it solve?
cards.answer: A static block (`static { ... }`) runs once during class evaluation, in source order alongside the static field initializers (it can read static fields declared before it). It solves complex multi-step initialization of static state that can't be expressed in a single initializer expression — for example using a loop, try/catch, or reading one static field to compute another.

cards.question: What does `typeof null` return, and why is it considered a historical bug?
cards.answer: `typeof null` returns `'object'`. This is a long-standing bug from JavaScript's first implementation where null's internal type tag was 0, the same tag used for objects. It was never fixed to avoid breaking existing code.
hints: It was a mistake in the original JS engine that cannot be fixed without breaking the web

cards.question: What does `Number.isFinite(value)` do differently from the global `isFinite(value)`?
cards.answer: `Number.isFinite` does NOT coerce its argument — it returns `false` for any non-number value. The global `isFinite` coerces with `Number()` first, so `isFinite('3')` returns `true` while `Number.isFinite('3')` returns `false`.

cards.question: What does `String.prototype.normalize` do, and why is it important for Unicode comparison?
cards.answer: `normalize(form)` converts a string to one of the four Unicode Normalization Forms: `'NFC'`, `'NFD'`, `'NFKC'`, or `'NFKD'`. The same visible character can be encoded as a single precomposed code point or as a base character plus combining marks. Without normalization, two strings that both render as `é` can compare unequal (`===` is `false`). Normalizing both to NFC (the default) makes such strings compare equal.

cards.question: Why does the default `Array.prototype.sort` comparator produce unexpected results when sorting numbers?
cards.answer: The default comparator converts elements to strings and sorts them lexicographically (by UTF-16 code unit). So `[10, 9, 1].sort()` yields `[1, 10, 9]` because `'10' < '9'` as strings. To sort numerically, provide a comparator: `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

cards.question: How do computed property keys work in object literals?
cards.answer: Computed property keys use square brackets `[]` in an object literal to evaluate an expression as the property name at creation time. For example: `const key = 'name'; const obj = { [key]: 'Alice' };` creates `{ name: 'Alice' }`. The expression's result is coerced to a string (or used directly if it is a symbol).
hints: Uses the same bracket syntax as property access

cards.question: What is an IIFE, and what problem does it traditionally solve?
cards.answer: An **Immediately Invoked Function Expression** (IIFE) is a function defined and called in one expression: `(function() { /* ... */ })()`. It creates a private scope, preventing variable leakage into the surrounding (global) scope. With `let`/`const` and ES modules this is less critical, but IIFEs remain useful for encapsulation and async initialization patterns.

cards.question: What does `.finally()` receive as its callback argument, and what does the callback's return value affect?
cards.answer: The `.finally()` callback receives **no arguments** — it has no access to the settled value or rejection reason. Its return value is normally ignored and the original settled value or rejection propagates unchanged. The exception: if the callback throws or returns a promise that rejects, the chain adopts that new rejection.

cards.question: How do you run two independent async operations in parallel with `async/await` instead of sequentially?
cards.answer:
Start both Promises before awaiting either, then await them together. For example:
```js
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]);
```
Awaiting each call sequentially (`await fetchA(); await fetchB()`) waits for the first to finish before starting the second.

cards.question: What does `yield*` do inside a generator, and how does it differ from `yield`?
cards.answer: `yield*` delegates to another iterable (or generator), forwarding each of its values to the outer generator's consumer. It is equivalent to iterating the inner iterable with a `for...of` loop and `yield`-ing each value. Unlike plain `yield`, it also evaluates to the inner generator's final `return` value as the result of the `yield*` expression.

cards.question: How does `Set` enforce uniqueness, and what does that mean for `NaN` values?
cards.answer: Set uses SameValueZero for uniqueness checks. Because SameValueZero treats `NaN` as equal to itself, a Set can only hold **one** `NaN` entry regardless of how many times it is added. For example: `new Set([NaN, NaN]).size === 1`.

cards.question: How does `Symbol.toPrimitive` differ from `valueOf` and `toString` in controlling type coercion?
cards.answer: `Symbol.toPrimitive` is called with a `hint` argument (`'number'`, `'string'`, or `'default'`) giving the object full context about which kind of conversion is being requested. `valueOf` and `toString` receive no such hint, so the object cannot distinguish contexts. If `Symbol.toPrimitive` is present, it takes precedence over both.

cards.question: What does a **namespace import** (`import * as ns from './mod.js'`) give you, and what are its limitations?
cards.answer: A namespace import creates a *module namespace object* — a sealed object whose properties are the module's named exports (plus `default` if one exists). Its properties are non-writable and non-configurable, so you cannot add, delete, or reassign them. It reflects live bindings, so `ns.counter` updates if the exporter reassigns `counter`. The default export is only accessible explicitly as `ns.default`.

cards.question: How does error handling work with `async/await`? How do you catch a rejection?
cards.answer: With `async/await` you wrap `await` calls in a `try/catch` block — a rejected promise causes the `await` expression to throw, and the `catch` clause receives the rejection reason. Alternatively, you can append `.catch()` directly on the returned promise from an `async` function call.
hints: await turns rejections into thrown exceptions

cards.question: Explain the month indexing gotcha when constructing a `Date` with `new Date(year, month, day)`.
cards.answer: `month` is **zero-indexed** (0 = January, 11 = December), but `day` is one-indexed. So `new Date(2024, 0, 1)` is 1 January 2024. Forgetting this is one of the most common `Date` bugs.

cards.question: What is variable shadowing and when can it cause subtle bugs?
cards.answer: Shadowing occurs when an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as one in an outer scope, hiding the outer binding within that inner scope. It can cause bugs when a developer intends to modify the outer variable but accidentally creates a new inner one, so the outer variable is never updated.

cards.question: How does replacing `var` with `let` in a `for` loop fix the stale-closure problem?
What is the difference between `Function.prototype.call` and `Function.prototype.apply` regarding argument passing?
cards.answer: `call(thisArg, arg1, arg2, ...)` passes arguments individually as a comma-separated list. `apply(thisArg, [arg1, arg2, ...])` passes arguments as a single array (or array-like object). Both invoke the function immediately with the specified `this`.

cards.question: What is property shadowing in JavaScript prototypes?
cards.answer: When an object defines a property with the same name as one on its prototype, the object's own property *shadows* the prototype's version. Any access through that object resolves to the own property, leaving the prototype's property unchanged. Example: if `obj.toString = () => 'custom'`, then `obj.toString()` calls the own version, not `Object.prototype.toString`.
hints: Own properties always win over inherited ones

cards.question: When must you call `super()` in a derived class constructor, and what happens if you omit it?
cards.answer: In a derived class (one that `extends` a base class), `super()` must be called before accessing `this` or returning from the constructor. Omitting it, or accessing `this` before it, throws a `ReferenceError` because `this` is uninitialized until the parent constructor runs.

cards.question: How does a primitive `string` differ from a `String` wrapper object in JavaScript?
cards.answer: A primitive string is an immutable scalar value; `typeof 'hello'` is `'string'`. A `String` wrapper object created with `new String('hello')` is an actual object; `typeof new String('hello')` is `'object'`. Primitives compared with `===` compare by value; `String` objects compare by reference. Wrapper objects are rarely needed in practice.

cards.question: How does the `+` operator decide whether to concatenate strings or add numbers?
cards.answer: The `+` operator calls `ToPrimitive` on both operands (with no preferred type, so hint is `'default'`, which most objects treat like `'number'`). If either resulting primitive is a string, it does string concatenation; otherwise it converts both to numbers and adds them. So `1 + '2'` is `'12'` but `1 + 2` is `3`.
hints: If either side is a string after coercion, concatenation wins.

cards.question: Explain what `toFixed(n)` does and one common pitfall developers encounter with it.
cards.answer: `toFixed(n)` returns a string with `n` decimal places, rounding the number. A common pitfall is that rounding can look wrong due to IEEE-754 representation: `(1.005).toFixed(2)` returns `'1.00'` instead of `'1.01'` because `1.005` cannot be stored exactly and is actually held as roughly `1.00499999999999989`, which rounds down.

cards.question: Explain `String.prototype.replaceAll` and how it differs from `replace` with a global regular expression.
cards.answer: `replaceAll(searchValue, replacement)` replaces every occurrence of `searchValue` (a string or regex) in one call. When `searchValue` is a string, `replace` only replaces the *first* match, while `replaceAll` replaces *all*. If a regex is passed to `replaceAll`, it *must* have the `g` flag, otherwise a `TypeError` is thrown. `replaceAll` was introduced in ES2021.

cards.question: What are sparse arrays (arrays with holes) and how do common iteration methods treat holes?
cards.answer: A sparse array has empty slots — indices with no assigned value, created via `new Array(3)` or `delete arr[i]`. Many iteration methods (`forEach`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`) skip holes entirely. Methods like `join` render them as empty strings (the same as `undefined`/`null`), and `flat` removes them. Holes differ from `undefined` values — `0 in new Array(3)` is `false`.

cards.question: What is the difference between an accessor property descriptor and a data property descriptor?
cards.answer: A data descriptor has `value` and `writable` attributes. An accessor descriptor has `get` and `set` attributes (functions called on read/write) instead. Both share `enumerable` and `configurable`. A single property cannot be both — mixing `value`/`writable` with `get`/`set` on the same descriptor throws a `TypeError`.

cards.question: What is currying, and how does it differ from partial application?
cards.answer: **Currying** transforms a function of multiple arguments into a chain of unary functions: `f(a, b, c)` becomes `f(a)(b)(c)`. **Partial application** fixes some arguments up front and returns a new function expecting the rest. Currying always produces unary functions at each step; partial application may return a function that still accepts multiple arguments.
hints: Unary means one argument at a time

cards.question: What is 'promise chaining' and why does it avoid the 'callback hell' problem?
cards.answer: Promise chaining is the practice of returning a new value (or promise) from `.then()` so the next `.then()` in the chain receives it. Because each `.then()` returns a new Promise, async operations compose as a flat sequence rather than deeply nested callbacks. Error handling is centralized in a single `.catch()` at the end of the chain.

cards.question: How do you handle errors from `await` expressions inside an `async` function?
How can you write an infinite generator in JavaScript, and why doesn't it block the program?
cards.answer: An infinite generator uses an unbounded loop with `yield` — e.g., `function* naturals() { let n = 0; while (true) yield n++; }`. It doesn't block because a generator is *lazy*: execution pauses at each `yield` and only resumes when the consumer calls `next()`. The consumer controls how many values it pulls.

cards.question: What is a `WeakMap` and why can it not be iterated or have its size inspected?
cards.answer: A `WeakMap` holds **weak references** to its keys, allowing the garbage collector to reclaim a key-value pair when there are no other references to the key. Because the set of live entries is non-deterministic (it depends on GC timing), exposing iteration or `.size` would produce unreliable, timing-dependent results, so the spec deliberately omits them.

cards.question: Why are symbol-keyed properties sometimes described as 'non-enumerable-ish', and which APIs can still see them?
cards.answer: Symbol keys are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys()`, and `JSON.stringify()` by default — hence 'non-enumerable-ish'. (Note `Object.assign()` *does* copy enumerable symbol-keyed properties.) `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols()` and `Reflect.ownKeys()` expose them. Symbols are not truly non-enumerable in the descriptor sense; a property created via assignment has `enumerable: true` unless explicitly set to `false`.

cards.question: What is the role of `module.exports` vs `exports` in CommonJS?
cards.answer: `module.exports` is the object that `require()` actually returns. `exports` starts as a reference to the same object, so `exports.foo = 1` works. But if you reassign `exports = { foo: 1 }`, you break the reference — the consumer still gets the original `module.exports`. Always reassign `module.exports` directly when exporting a single value or replacing the whole export object.

cards.question: What is `AggregateError` and when is it used?
cards.answer: `AggregateError` (ES2021) is a built-in error subclass that holds multiple errors in its `.errors` array. It is thrown by `Promise.any()` when **all** promises in the iterable reject, bundling every rejection reason together. You can also construct it manually: `new AggregateError([err1, err2], 'All failed')`.

cards.question: What does `structuredClone` do, and how does it differ from `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))`?
cards.answer: `structuredClone` performs a deep clone using the structured clone algorithm. Unlike the JSON round-trip it correctly handles `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `ArrayBuffer`, typed arrays, circular references, and `undefined` values. It does **not** clone functions or DOM nodes (it throws a `DataCloneError`).

cards.question: What does the `void` operator do?
cards.answer: `void expr` evaluates `expr` and then always yields `undefined`, discarding the operand's value. It is occasionally used to obtain a guaranteed `undefined` (e.g. `void 0`) or to evaluate an expression for its side effect while ignoring the result.

cards.question: Why can `Array.isArray(value)` be more reliable than `value instanceof Array`?
cards.answer: `instanceof Array` checks the prototype chain against *this* realm's `Array`, so it returns `false` for an array created in another realm (e.g. an `<iframe>` or a worker). `Array.isArray()` recognises array exotic objects across realms, so it works no matter which context created the array.

cards.question: What does the comma operator evaluate to, as in `(a, b, c)`?
cards.answer: The comma operator evaluates each operand left to right and returns the value of the **last** one, so `(1, 2, 3)` is `3`. It shows up most often in `for`-loop headers; elsewhere it is rarely needed.
`var` declarations are hoisted and initialized to `undefined` before execution begins, so `console.log(x)` runs before the assignment and prints `undefined`.

Each call to `makeAdder` creates a new closure that independently captures its own `x` parameter. `add5` closes over `x = 5`, so `add5(3)` returns `8`. `add10` closes over `x = 10`, so `add10(3)` returns `13`.
In strict mode, calling a plain function without a receiver leaves `this` as `undefined` rather than the global object.

cards.question: What does `typeof Symbol('id')` return?
cards.answer: `typeof` applied to a Symbol value returns the string `'symbol'`. Symbols are a primitive type introduced in ES2015.

cards.question: What does `[] == ![]` evaluate to in JavaScript?
cards.answer: `![]` is `false` (because `[]` is truthy). Then `[] == false` triggers coercion: `false` becomes `0`, `[]` becomes `''` via ToPrimitive, then `''` becomes `0`. So `0 == 0` is `true`.
hints: ![] is false; then both sides get coerced to numbers.

cards.question: What does `Number.isInteger(1.0)` return?
cards.answer: `1.0` and `1` are the same value in JavaScript's double type. `Number.isInteger` checks whether the value is a number with no fractional part, so it returns `true` for `1.0`.

cards.question: What does `'abcdef'.slice(2, -1)` return?
cards.answer: `slice(2, -1)` starts at index 2 (`'c'`) and ends at `length - 1` (index 5, exclusive), so it returns characters at indices 2, 3, 4: `'cde'`.

cards.question: Which of the following methods does NOT mutate the original array?
cards.answer: `slice` returns a shallow copy of the portion of the array; it never changes the original. `splice`, `sort`, and `fill` all mutate the array in place.

cards.question: What is the default value of the `writable` attribute when a property is created via `Object.defineProperty` without specifying it?
cards.answer: With `Object.defineProperty`, omitted boolean descriptor attributes (`writable`, `enumerable`, `configurable`) default to `false`. This is unlike normal property assignment, where those attributes all default to `true`.
hints: Defaults are different from assignment-created properties

cards.answer: Default parameter expressions are evaluated at call time and can reference earlier parameters. `b` defaults to `a * 2`, which is `3 * 2 = 6`.

cards.question:
Given the following code, what is logged?
```js
Promise.resolve('a')
  .then(v => v + 'b')
  .then(v => { throw new Error('stop'); })
  .then(v => v + 'c')
  .catch(e => e.message)
  .then(v => console.log(v));
```
cards.answer: Throwing inside `.then()` rejects the chain, skipping the next `.then()`. The `.catch()` handles the error and returns `e.message` ('stop'), which is then passed to the final `.then()` and logged.

choices.text: Nothing is logged; the error is unhandled

cards.question: What does `Symbol('foo') === Symbol('foo')` evaluate to?
cards.answer: Each call to `Symbol()` produces a completely unique primitive, regardless of the description string. The description is only a human-readable label for debugging; it plays no role in equality checks.

choices.text: `true`, because both symbols have the same description
`false`, because each `Symbol()` call creates a unique value
`true`, because string-equal descriptions imply symbol equality
It throws a `TypeError` — symbols cannot be compared with `===`

cards.question: Which statement correctly re-exports a named export `add` from `./math.js` without binding it locally?
cards.answer: `export { add } from './math.js'` is the aggregator syntax that re-exports without creating a local binding. The other forms are either syntax errors or require a prior `import`.
`finally` always executes and its `return` overrides the `try` block's `return`. So `return 2` wins and the function returns `2`.

cards.question:
What does the following expression evaluate to?
```js
JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: undefined, c: null })
```
cards.answer: `undefined` property values are dropped entirely from the JSON output, while `null` is a valid JSON value and is kept. So `b` disappears and `c` remains.

cards.question: Which keyword(s) create a block-scoped variable?
cards.answer: Both `let` and `const` are block-scoped; their bindings are confined to the nearest enclosing `{}`. `var` is function-scoped (or global), not block-scoped.

cards.question: Which technique creates a **new binding** for each loop iteration, fixing the classic closure-in-loop bug without using `let`?
cards.answer: An IIFE creates a new function scope on each iteration. Passing `i` as a parameter makes a fresh local copy for each closure. `const` cannot be used in a `for` loop increment header, and the other options do not fix the binding problem.

choices.text: Wrap the callback in an IIFE that receives `i` as a parameter
Use `const` instead of `var` in the loop head
Move the `setTimeout` call outside the loop
Add `'use strict'` at the top of the file

cards.question: Which statement correctly describes `Object.create(null)`?
cards.answer: Passing `null` to `Object.create` explicitly sets `[[Prototype]]` to `null`, producing a truly bare object with no inherited methods like `toString` or `hasOwnProperty`.

choices.text: It creates an object with no prototype (`[[Prototype]]` is null)
It creates an object whose prototype is `Object.prototype`
It throws a TypeError because null is not a valid prototype
It creates an object identical to `{}`

hints: Useful for pure dictionaries

cards.question: Which statement about `static` methods is correct?
cards.answer: Static methods are defined on the class constructor object itself, so you call `ClassName.method()`. They are not on the instance's prototype chain, so `instance.method()` is `undefined`. (Static methods can freely reference other static members via `this` inside the method.)

choices.text: They are available on instances via `this`
They are called on the class itself, not on instances
They are stored on each instance's own properties
They cannot access other static members

cards.question: Which of the following creates a primitive value (not a wrapper object)?
cards.answer: Calling `String('hello')` without `new` is a type-conversion function and returns the primitive string `'hello'`. Using `new String(...)`, `new Boolean(...)`, or `new Number(...)` creates wrapper objects.

cards.question: What is the result of `null == undefined`?
cards.answer: The Abstract Equality Comparison spec has a special rule: `null == undefined` is always `true`, and neither coerces to any other value in this comparison. They are only `==` to each other, not to `0`, `false`, or `''`.
